candidates.statement: As discussed below, FDA considers FFRs and reusable respirators used to prevent wearer 44 exposure to pathogenic biological airborne particulates to be devices intended for a medical 45 purpose and within the scope of this guidance . The healthcare setting presents unique respiratory 46 risks that do not ordinarily arise in other environments . Healthcare settings are necessarily places 47 whe re people with respiratory illness seek treatment, presenting risk of exposure to respiratory 48 disease to people working in such facilities. D isease pathogens can transmit in the healthcare 49 setting through sneez es or cough s and through droplets or sprays of infectious body fluids . 50 Treatment for respiratory diseas e, including intubation , extubation or a erosolized administration 51 of medications (e.g. nebulizer treatments) , may create or cause airborne particulat es and/or 52 pathogens . Other hospital activities require equipment that may aerosolize pathogens, including 53 clinical, surgical, and laboratory procedures utilizing b one saws, centrifuges, and blenders . In 54 addition, cleaning and disinfecting healthcare facilities can create potentially harmful airborne 55 particulates. The CDC has stated: “T he hospital environment contains hazards such as bacteria, 56 viruses, and chemicals that may be inhaled by personnel and cause injury or illness . . . 57 H ealthcare personnel who care for patients with ATD s [ aerosol transmissible diseases ] must 58 work in close proximity to the source of the hazard; even with controls in place, they are likely to 59 have a higher risk of inhaling infectious aerosols (droplets and particles) than the general 60 public. ” 8

candidates.statement: Class III devices are subject to premarket approval (PMA) requirements under section 515 of the FD&C Act. PMA is the required process of scientific and regulatory review to assess the safety and effectiveness of class III devices.
candidates.context: FDA is aware that healthcare personnel have use d , 17 and will continue to use r espirator s in 112 healthcare setti ngs for medical purposes including protection from transmission of respiratory 113 process and regardless of the risks they pose, unless they are substantially equivalent to certain other devices (e.g., predicate devices which have been classified into class I or class II) , FDA has re classified the device into class I or class II in response to a petition , or FDA has granted a De Novo request classifying the device into class I or class II . A class III device that is marketed without complying with applicable PMA requirements is adulterated under section 501(f) of the FD&C Act.
